inlines.text: applies trigonometric ratios to solve right-angled triangle problems

Apply trigonometry to solve right-angled triangle problems
Apply trigonometry to find the lengths of unknown sides in right-angled triangles with a given angle including angles in degrees and minutes
Apply trigonometry to find the size of unknown angles in right-angled triangles including in degrees and minutes
Solve a variety of practical problems involving trigonometric ratios in right-angled triangles

spec.description: Right triangle with horizontal lower leg 3, vertical right leg 4, right angle at lower right and theta at upper right. Ordinary source blue outlines use house black.
spec.mathematics: Perpendicular legs have lengths 3 and 4. The unlabelled hypotenuse is opposite the right angle; the leg of length 3 is opposite theta.
spec.answerVisibility: Only the given lengths, right-angle mark and theta are visible.

answer.worked:
Let $h$ be the hypotenuse.
$$\begin{align*}h^2&=3^2+4^2\\h^2&=25\\h&=5\end{align*}$$
Relative to $\theta$, $O=3$, $A=4$ and $H=5$.
$$\begin{align*}\sin\theta&=\frac{O}{H}=\frac35\\\cos\theta&=\frac{A}{H}=\frac45\\\tan\theta&=\frac{O}{A}=\frac34\end{align*}$$

spec.description: Narrow rotated triangle with right angle at upper right, short upper leg 7, long right leg 24 and theta at the bottom. Ordinary outlines and labels use black.

spec.answerVisibility: The hypotenuse and all ratio answers remain hidden.

answer.worked:
Let $h$ be the hypotenuse.
$$\begin{align*}h^2&=7^2+24^2\\h^2&=625\\h&=25\end{align*}$$
Relative to $\theta$, $O=7$, $A=24$ and $H=25$.
$$\begin{align*}\sin\theta&=\frac{O}{H}=\frac7{25}\\\cos\theta&=\frac{A}{H}=\frac{24}{25}\\\tan\theta&=\frac{O}{A}=\frac7{24}\end{align*}$$

spec.answerVisibility: Only source givens and angle marks are visible; no hypotenuse or ratio answer is printed.

answer.worked:
Let $h$ be the hypotenuse.
$$\begin{align*}h^2&=9^2+12^2\\h^2&=225\\h&=15\end{align*}$$
Relative to $\theta$, $O=9$, $A=12$ and $H=15$.
$$\begin{align*}\sin\theta&=\frac{O}{H}=\frac9{15}=\frac35\\\cos\theta&=\frac{A}{H}=\frac{12}{15}=\frac45\\\tan\theta&=\frac{O}{A}=\frac9{12}=\frac34\end{align*}$$

answer.worked:
Let $h$ be the hypotenuse.
$$\begin{align*}h^2&=8^2+6^2\\h^2&=100\\h&=10\end{align*}$$
Relative to $\theta$, $O=8$, $A=6$ and $H=10$.
$$\begin{align*}\sin\theta&=\frac{O}{H}=\frac8{10}=\frac45\\\cos\theta&=\frac{A}{H}=\frac6{10}=\frac35\\\tan\theta&=\frac{O}{A}=\frac86=\frac43\end{align*}$$

children.prompt: For a triangle with a $30^{\circ}$ interior angle, what is the ratio of:

answer.worked: The opposite side is half the hypotenuse, so $\sin 30^{\circ}=\frac{1}{2}=0.5$.
For any right-angled triangle with a $30^{\circ}$ angle, $\frac{\text{Adjacent}}{\text{Hypotenuse}}=\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\approx0.87$.
For any right-angled triangle with a $30^{\circ}$ angle, $\frac{\text{Opposite}}{\text{Adjacent}}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\approx0.58$.

children.prompt: Do these values change if you make the triangle larger or smaller?

answer.short: No. The ratios stay the same.
answer.worked: The triangles are similar. Enlarging or reducing the triangle multiplies every side by the same scale factor, so each ratio stays the same.

children.prompt: Type $\sin 30^{\circ}$, $\cos 30^{\circ}$, and $\tan 30^{\circ}$ into your calculator. Use degree mode. Round non-terminating decimals to 2 decimal places.

answer.short: The calculator values match the side ratios.
answer.worked: Each calculator value agrees with the corresponding side ratio measured in the right-angled triangle, allowing for rounding.

content.prompt: A right-angled triangle has cosine ratio of $\frac{1}{2}$. Every side of the triangle is made 3 times longer. What is the new cosine ratio? Explain your answer using a diagram if necessary.

answer.short: $\frac{1}{2}$. The triangles are similar, so the cosine ratio is unchanged.
answer.worked:
Let $A$ be the adjacent side and $H$ the hypotenuse.
$$\begin{align*}\text{New cosine ratio}&=\frac{3A}{3H}\\&=\frac{A}{H}\\&=\frac{1}{2}\end{align*}$$
The triangles are similar. Multiplying every side by the same factor leaves the ratio unchanged.

answer.short: Yes. $\tan45^{\circ}=\frac{O}{A}=1$, so $O=A$ and the triangle is isosceles.
answer.worked:
Let $O$ and $A$ be the opposite and adjacent sides relative to the $45^{\circ}$ angle.
$$\begin{align*}\tan45^{\circ}&=\frac{O}{A}\\\frac{O}{A}&=1\\O&=A\end{align*}$$
The two shorter sides are equal, so the triangle is always isosceles.

content.prompt: Explain why it is impossible to have a right-angled triangle with these properties.

answer.short: Impossible: $\dfrac{O}{A}>0$ because both side lengths are positive.
answer.worked:
$$\tan\theta=\frac{O}{A}=-1$$
This would require one of $O$ and $A$ to be negative, but side lengths are positive.

answer.short: Impossible: this requires $O=H$, but the hypotenuse is longer than either other side.
answer.worked:
$$\begin{align*}\frac{O}{H}&=1\\O&=H\end{align*}$$
This is impossible because the hypotenuse is longer than either other side.

answer.short: Impossible: this requires $A=0$, but a triangle's side lengths are positive.
answer.worked:
$$\begin{align*}\frac{A}{H}&=0\\A&=0\end{align*}$$
A triangle cannot have a side of length zero.

answer.short: Impossible: this requires $O>H$ or $A>H$, but the hypotenuse is the longest side.
answer.worked:
For $\sin\theta>1$:
$$\begin{align*}\frac{O}{H}&>1\\O&>H\end{align*}$$
For $\cos\theta>1$:
$$\begin{align*}\frac{A}{H}&>1\\A&>H\end{align*}$$
Both are impossible because the hypotenuse is the longest side.

answer.worked:

content.prompt: $M$ is the midpoint of $AB$. Determine whether the angle $\angle ACM$ is exactly half of angle $ACB$. Give calculated angles to 1 d.p.

spec.description: Triangle CAB with horizontal CA, vertical AB, midpoint M, segments CB and CM, a midpoint dot and a right-angle square at A. Ordinary source blue strokes are rendered black under house style.
spec.mathematics: CA = 6 m; AM = MB = 2 m; CA is perpendicular to AB; M is the midpoint of AB.
spec.answerVisibility: Only source givens are visible; no calculated angles appear in the question diagram.

answer.short: No. $\angle ACM\approx18.4^\circ$ and $\angle ACB\approx33.7^\circ$, so $\angle ACM$ is not half of $\angle ACB$.
answer.worked:
$AB=2+2=4\,\mathrm{m}$.

$$\begin{align*}
\tan\angle ACM&=\frac{AM}{AC}\\
\tan\angle ACM&=\frac{2}{6}\\
\angle ACM&=\tan^{-1}\left(\frac{2}{6}\right)\\
\angle ACM&\approx18.43495^\circ\\
\tan\angle ACB&=\frac{AB}{AC}\\
\tan\angle ACB&=\frac{4}{6}\\
\angle ACB&=\tan^{-1}\left(\frac{4}{6}\right)\\
\angle ACB&\approx33.69007^\circ
\end{align*}$$

Half of $\angle ACB$ is approximately $16.84503^\circ$, which differs from $\angle ACM$. Therefore, $\angle ACM$ is not exactly half of $\angle ACB$.

Let $L$ be the ladder length in cm.

spec.description: Bird and person silhouettes replaced by editable role labels; both heights, dashed projections and right-angle marks retained.

answer.worked:
The height difference is $2450-187=2263\text{ cm}$.
$$\begin{align*}\tan62^\circ&=\frac{2263}{d}\\d\tan62^\circ&=2263\\d&=\frac{2263}{\tan62^\circ}\\d&\approx1203.3\text{ cm}\end{align*}$$

spec.description: Symmetric roof triangle with both base angles, full-span dimension, dashed altitude and external right-slope dimension; decorative chimney omitted.

spec.answerVisibility: The half-span and slant-height answer are not supplied.

answer.worked:
The equal base angles make the roof triangle isosceles, so the altitude bisects the span: $1600\div2=800\text{ cm}$.
$$\begin{align*}\cos40^\circ&=\frac{800}{w}\\w\cos40^\circ&=800\\w&=\frac{800}{\cos40^\circ}\\w&\approx1044.3\text{ cm}\end{align*}$$

spec.description: Unshaded leaning tower outline with ground, dashed vertical projection, right-angle mark and horizontal offset. The source's unattached 90 m label remains between the projection and leaning side.

answer.worked:
If $90\text{ m}$ is the vertical height:
$$\begin{align*}\tan\theta&=\frac{90}{3}\\\theta&=\tan^{-1}\left(\frac{90}{3}\right)\\\theta&\approx88^\circ5'\end{align*}$$
If $90\text{ m}$ is the leaning length:
$$\begin{align*}\cos\theta&=\frac{3}{90}\\\theta&=\cos^{-1}\left(\frac{3}{90}\right)\\\theta&\approx88^\circ5'\end{align*}$$
Both interpretations give the supplied answer to the nearest minute.

content.prompt:
Toby constructed two isosceles right triangles.
He says that when the two short sides are the same the angle $\theta$ is always $45^\circ$.

children.label: a
children.prompt: Show he is correct, using trigonometry in the two triangles.

spec.description: Equal perpendicular legs, Roman numeral I, and the acute theta at the bottom right.
spec.mathematics: Both legs are 12 cm; bottom-left angle is right.
spec.answerVisibility: The unknown angle is not evaluated.

spec.description: Second equal-leg triangle, positioned to the right of I for comparison.
spec.mathematics: Both legs are 17 cm; bottom-left angle is right.
spec.answerVisibility: The unknown angle is not evaluated.

answer.worked:
Triangle I:
$$\begin{align*}\tan\theta&=\frac{12}{12}\\\theta&=\tan^{-1}(1)\\\theta&=45^\circ\end{align*}$$
Triangle II:
$$\begin{align*}\tan\theta&=\frac{17}{17}\\\theta&=\tan^{-1}(1)\\\theta&=45^\circ\end{align*}$$
Both triangles have $\theta=45^\circ$, so Toby is correct.

children.label: b
children.prompt: Show he is correct, using properties of isosceles triangles and angle sum of a triangle.

answer.short: The two acute angles are equal. $2\theta+90^\circ=180^\circ$, so $\theta=45^\circ$.

In $\triangle ADC$, $\angle ADC=25^{\circ}+25^{\circ}=50^{\circ}$.

answer.worked:
In $\triangle ABP$:

In $\triangle APC$:

In $\triangle PQR$:

spec.description: Regular hexagon with horizontal top and bottom edges, equal-side ticks on all six edges, A at the leftmost vertex, C at the bottom-left vertex and B vertically above C on the horizontal diameter. Dashed red constructions join A to the opposite vertex and B to C. The interior angle at the top-left vertex is 120 degrees, and the lower-right edge is labelled 10 cm. Decorative blue outlines are replaced by ordinary black ink.
spec.mathematics: Every side is 10 cm. Triangle ABC is right-angled at B; AC is a hexagon side. The horizontal diameter bisects the 120-degree interior angle at A, giving angle BAC = 60 degrees.
spec.answerVisibility: Only source givens and constructions are visible; no calculated lengths or 60-degree solution annotation.

children.label: a
children.prompt: Find the length of $BC$ to 2 decimal places.

answer.worked:
The horizontal diameter bisects the interior angle at $A$, so $\angle BAC=60^{\circ}$.
$$\begin{align*}\sin60^{\circ}&=\frac{BC}{10}\\BC&=10\sin60^{\circ}\\BC&\approx8.66\text{ cm}\end{align*}$$

children.label: c
children.prompt: Find the distance between the parallel sides to 1 decimal place.

answer.worked:
By symmetry, the perpendicular distance between the parallel sides is $2BC$.
$$\begin{align*}2BC&=20\sin60^{\circ}\\2BC&\approx17.3\text{ cm}\end{align*}$$

answer.worked:
The horizontal distance between opposite vertices consists of two lengths equal to $AB$ and one length equal to a side.
$$5+10+5=20\text{ cm}$$

content.prompt: A bridge spans a river, and the two identical sections of the bridge, each of length $x$ metres, can be raised to allow tall boats to pass. When the two sections are fully raised, they are each inclined at $50^\circ$ to the horizontal, and there is an 18-metre gap between them, as shown in the diagram. Calculate the width of the river in metres, correct to one decimal place.

spec.description: Symmetric raised bridge sections, dashed horizontal gap and baseline, and circular swing arcs terminating at the common closed-position midpoint. Ordinary source marks are rendered black without shading.
spec.mathematics: Each bridge section has length x. Each rises at 50 degrees to the horizontal. The horizontal distance between raised endpoints is 18 m. The closed sections meet at the baseline midpoint, so the river width is 2x. Drawing coordinates express these relationships without introducing additional numerical givens.
spec.answerVisibility: Only source givens are visible; no calculated width or section length is shown.

answer.worked:
The closed sections meet at the midpoint, so the river is $2x$ metres wide. Each raised section has horizontal projection $x\cos50^\circ$.
$$\begin{align*}
2x-2x\cos50^\circ &= 18\\
2x(1-\cos50^\circ) &= 18\\
2x &= \frac{18}{1-\cos50^\circ}\\
2x &\approx 50.4\,\mathrm{m}
\end{align*}$$
The river is $50.4\,\mathrm{m}$ wide, correct to one decimal place.

spec.description: Unshaded triangle QPS, right-angled at P, with perpendicular altitude PR to the horizontal baseline QS. All ordinary outlines and labels use black. Coordinates are schematic and enforce both right angles without asserting numerical measurements.
spec.mathematics: Q, R and S are collinear in that order; PR is perpendicular to QS; PQ is perpendicular to PS; QR=a, RS=b, PR=h and angle PQS=theta.
spec.answerVisibility: All vertex names, side labels, theta and both right-angle markers are permanent student-visible givens.

answer.worked:
In right-angled triangle $QPR$, $\angle QPR=90^\circ-\theta$. Since $\angle QPS=90^\circ$,
$$\begin{align*}\angle RPS&=90^\circ-(90^\circ-\theta)\\&=\theta.\end{align*}$$

Using opposite over adjacent in triangles $QPR$ and $PRS$, respectively:
$$\begin{align*}\tan\theta&=\frac{h}{a}\\\tan\theta&=\frac{b}{h}.\end{align*}$$

Equate the two expressions for $\tan\theta$ and multiply both sides by $ah$:
$$\begin{align*}\frac{h}{a}&=\frac{b}{h}\\h^2&=ab\\ab&=h^2.\end{align*}$$

entries.description:
Syllabus Content
MA5-TRG-C-01 applies trigonometric ratios to solve right-angled triangle problems

Demonstrate and explain the constancy of trigonometric ratios for a given angle in a right-angled triangle
• Identify and label the hypotenuse, adjacent and opposite sides with respect to a given angle in a right-angled triangle in any orientation
• Define the sine, cosine and tangent ratios for angles in right-angled triangles and use trigonometric notation sin θ, cos θ, tan θ
• Identify the sine, cosine and tangent ratios in a right-angled triangle
• Verify the constancy of the sine, cosine and tangent ratios for a given angle by applying knowledge of similar right-angled triangles
• Find approximations of the trigonometric ratios for a given angle
• Find the size of an angle given one of the trigonometric ratios for the angle using digital tools

Apply trigonometry to solve right-angled triangle problems
• Apply trigonometry to find the lengths of unknown sides in right-angled triangles with a given angle including angles in degrees and minutes
• Apply trigonometry to find the size of unknown angles in right-angled triangles including in degrees and minutes
• Solve a variety of practical problems involving trigonometric ratios in right-angled triangles

  ○ Ten ones are ten. Ten tens are a hundred. Ten hundreds is a thousand…
• Angles use the sexagesimal system, based on sixties.
  ○ Sixty seconds are a minute. Sixty minutes are a degree.
Three-row definition table, in order: Degree ° — 1/360 of a turn; Minute ′ — 1/60 of a degree; Second ″ — 1/60 of a minute.
